synopsis: Lidar remains an option rather than a confirmed sensor for the heavy off-road automatic braking system, and ISO 16001:2017 has no dedicated lidar annex; lidar also should not be described as approved under MSHA 30 CFR 77.410, although it could qualify as “another effective device” [f2035, f6625, f2069, f2235]. Rain and fog are the best-validated lidar simulation cases, but the evidence is on-road: model agreement depends on rain distributions, signal processing and sensor imperfections, and mismatch increases as fog visibility falls [f4412, f7557, f4417, f7821]. Target properties strongly affect performance: 2023 field measurements found aluminium and steel targets unobserved at 20–30 m in rain of 30–40 mm/h and fog visibility below 50 m, while retroreflective targets retained at least 74% of clear-weather point count [f6382, f6383]. Dust is identified as the biggest off-road lidar gap: field evidence shows returns from cloud leading edges, effects beginning around 71–74% atmospheric transmittance with substantial variability, and published de-dusting results limited to single datasets [f12498, f10559, f10560, f10427]. Planning therefore still requires physical correlation for weather, reflectivity, contamination, ghost returns and scanner timing, supported by surveyed targets, reference lidar with RTK-GNSS/INS, and human-audited auto-labels; lidar stimulation, especially for solid-state devices, remains a gap [f1741, f5197, f5192].
